```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")) # CRAN re-check skips the computing
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 72)
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

A survey respondent stands for many people, and not the same number each: the final weight says
how many. The weights fix the estimate; the design (how the sample was drawn) fixes its
uncertainty, and ignoring it usually understates the interval. `svydes()` records the
design, `svyest()` gives means, totals, proportions and ratios with design-based
standard errors, and `svycmp()` tests differences between groups.

## Two ways to the variance

Public-use files from Statistics Canada and Health Canada ship **replicate weights**: hundreds of
alternative weight columns, each a resampled version of the design. The estimate is recomputed
under each and the spread of those estimates is the variance. Other surveys ship the **strata and
primary sampling units** (PSUs), and the variance comes from Taylor linearization.

```{r design}
set.seed(1)
n <- 600
d <- data.frame(region = sample(c("north", "south", "east"), n, replace = TRUE),
                age = sample(c("15-24", "25-49", "50+"), n, replace = TRUE),
                used = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3), drinks = rpois(n, 3), w = runif(n, 40, 160))
# a stratified design: variance by linearization
lin <- svydes(d, w = "w", strata = "region")
lin
# a replicate design: 200 bootstrap weights, made here by resampling within region
reps <- sapply(1:200, function(r) {
  m <- numeric(n)
  for (g in unique(d$region)) {
    i <- which(d$region == g)
    m[i] <- tabulate(sample(length(i), replace = TRUE), length(i)) * length(i) / (length(i) - 1)
  }
  d$w * m
})
repdes <- svydes(d, w = "w", reps = reps, type = "bootstrap")
repdes
```

## Estimates by domain

A domain (a region, an age group) is estimated inside the whole design: a respondent outside it
counts zero, but stays in the design. That is what makes the subgroup's variance right.

```{r estimate}
e <- svyest(repdes, d, "used", by = "age", stat = "proportion", lvls = "1")
e
plot(e)
svyest(lin, d, "drinks", by = "region")
```

Proportions get the modified Wilson interval of SAS PROC SURVEYFREQ (the effective sample size
\(n/\mathrm{Deff}\), adjusted for the design's degrees of freedom and never above \(n\)); it
stays inside 0 to 100% and behaves near the ends. Domains with fewer than 30 respondents are
flagged, the rule Health Canada uses to suppress estimates in its data tool; here nothing is
withheld, and the flag travels with the row.

## Comparing groups

Two overlapping intervals do not mean two groups are the same, and two separate intervals leave
out the covariance between the estimates. `svycmp()` takes the difference within the
design:

```{r compare}
cmp <- svycmp(repdes, d, "used", by = "region", stat = "proportion", lvls = "1",
                      ref = "north")
cmp
plot(cmp)
```

## The Canadian Substance Use Survey, against the published figures

CSUS 2023 ships 1,000 **mean bootstrap** weights, each the average of 12 bootstrap weights, so the
bootstrap variance is multiplied by 12 (Health Canada's technical notes; the same as Fay's BRR
with \(\rho = 1 - 1/\sqrt{12}\)). The public-use file and its weights are on data.rmorie.com
(sign in once with `rmbl login`), where `dload()` checks each table against the
SHA-256 its manifest lists:

```{r csus, eval = FALSE}
a <- dload("csus_2023/pumf")        # 36,180 respondents
b <- dload("csus_2023/bootstrap")   # PUMF_ID, WGT_PUMF and BWGT1 ... BWGT1000
```

Or, without signing in, from Health Canada's own copies on the Open Government Portal (the
same files, 612 MB for the weights):

```{r csus-open, eval = FALSE}
src <- "https://open.canada.ca/data/dataset/65e2d45e-efc6-4c29-9a9b-db59bc96aa0e/resource"
pumf <- file.path(tempdir(), "csus2023_pumf_final.csv")
bwt <- file.path(tempdir(), "csus2023_pumf_bwt.csv")
bldl(paste0(src, "/c2c1795b-4501-49ba-9dd1-5b8360cc3b2e/download/",
                           "csus2023_pumf_final.csv"), pumf)
bldl(paste0(src, "/7d19d47a-5f42-4447-b735-aa4d677ad5ed/download/",
                           "csus2023_pumf_bwt.csv"), bwt)
a <- utils::read.csv(pumf)
b <- utils::read.csv(bwt)
# With rmorie installed, the same two files come from
# rmorie::morie_load_dataset() with the keys "cu23mf" and "cu23bt".
```

Either way, the design and the lifetime cannabis question are:

```{r csus-estimate, eval = FALSE}
a$can <- ifelse(a$CAN_Q01 < 0, NA, a$CAN_Q01)   # -8: not stated
des <- svydes(a, w = "WGT_PUMF", reps = b, id = "PUMF_ID",
                     type = "meanboot", msize = 12)
svyest(des, a, "can", stat = "proportion", lvls = c("1", "2"))
```

Run on 13 October 2026 (1.6 seconds for the 1,000 replicates), against Health Infobase's
published table:

| Lifetime cannabis use | Published % | Published 95% CI | Here % | Here 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yes, just once | 9.907782 | 9.544212 to 10.28363 | 9.907816 | 9.522047 to 10.30743 |
| Yes, more than once | 53.192923 | 52.677340 to 53.70783 | 53.193086 | 52.677503 to 53.70799 |

The percentages agree to the fourth decimal, and so does the second interval, whose design
effect is below one so the interval is the plain Wilson one at the 36,024 respondents. The first
interval is slightly wider here: Health Canada computed from its master file, and the public-use
weights are not identical to it (the percentages differ in the fifth significant digit).

## When you only have the published table

Often there is no microdata, only the published table: an estimate and its 95% limits for each
group. The limits carry the design. A standard error is the limits' width over \(2z\), and it
includes the design effect of the survey's weights and clusters. `scests()` puts each
Statistics Canada estimate beside its limits. `indgap()`, `dstntst()` and
`ordcmp()` then compare groups from them.

They treat the groups as independent samples. Disjoint domains of one survey nearly are, but not
exactly, since they share strata and clusters. The exact comparison needs the bootstrap weights,
which Statistics Canada holds in its Research Data Centres.

Perceived mental health of First Nations, Metis and Inuit adults living off reserve, 2019/2022
(table 13-10-0924-01):

```{r published-only}
h <- indiex("health")
mh <- h[h$period == "2019/2022" & h$age == "Total, 18 years and over" &
          h$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]
indgap(mh, "group", "estimate", "lower", "upper", qual = "quality")[
  , c("group", "difference", "diflo", "difup")]
dstntst(mh[mh$group != "Non-Indigenous", ], "group", "estimate", "lower", "upper")
```

## Linearization or replicates, the same answer

On the same data the two routes agree closely when the replicates come from the same design:

```{r agree}
rbind(linearization = svyest(lin, d, "drinks")[, c("estimate", "se")],
      bootstrap = svyest(repdes, d, "drinks")[, c("estimate", "se")])
```

Every variance formula here is checked in the package tests against the survey package to machine
precision: linearized means, totals, ratios, proportions and domains with a finite population
correction; JK1, bootstrap and Fay replicate designs; and differences between domains.
